verdicts.note: The facts check out. Elson and Römer (HotNets-I, 28-29 Oct 2002) contains the post-facto quote word for word. Quinn's May 2023 drawback quote, the TrustedTime boot limit and Apple's 35F9.1 exception are also word for word. A second anchor is a good idea, and it does let TrustedTime leave the first release; Google itself says TrustedTime 'does not guarantee complete safety'. The mechanism as written is not safe. It computes 'server receipt minus an elapsed value the phone reports', and that value has no signature and no freshness bound. F5's own threat (an iPhone student who trusts a user-installed root CA) can edit the upload or hold it back. If the student also reboots before check-in, the forward anchor is gone, the backward anchor alone sets the record time, and the edited value gives a 'verified' late record. Even without MITM, the upload delay is never measured and pushes the computed time later.
verdicts.correction: Build the send-time anchor with F5's own mechanism instead of server receipt. Right before uploading, the phone requests a fresh certificate bound to a nonce (counter read when the request is sent, reply within the cap). The device key then signs (record id, that certificate, counter time elapsed from the record to that request). The server computes record time = certificate time minus the signed elapsed time. The allowance is that request's round trip plus 100 ppm of the elapsed time. If the signature or the nonce check fails, the record stays 'saat doğrulanamadı'. Dropping TrustedTime stays valid.

evidence.quote: In a packet delay manipulation scenario, an MITM attacker receives protocol packets and relays them to their destination after adding a maliciously computed delay.
You must manually turn on trust for SSL/TLS when you install a profile that is sent to you via email or downloaded from a website.
In contrast, we advocate post-facto synchronization, where clocks run unsynchronized at their own natural rates.
While TrustedTime makes it more difficult for users to manipulate the time accessed by your app, it does not guarantee complete safety.

verdicts.note: All five Apple sources check out (2018-10, 2023-05, 2025-02, 2025-12, 2026-07). Two independent sources agree. Chromium's iOS clock code says KERN_BOOTTIME is updated whenever the system clock changes. Apple's Libc computes CLOCK_MONOTONIC as gettimeofday minus boot time. Two precision notes. (1) Quinn's 'initial value' remark is about clocks built on the CPU counter (CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW). The plan's CLOCK_MONOTONIC does restart near zero. Even so, a 'counter went backwards' test misses a reboot once uptime passes the stored value, so the finding's conclusion stands. (2) The finding leaves out some implementation limits. Semaphore names are capped at 31 UTF-8 characters (PSEMNAMLEN), so the App Group ID must be short. Quinn's sample returns an 'unknown' state on other errors, and that state should count as a restart. EAS registers App Group IDs automatically only with an Apple cookie login run locally, not with an App Store Connect API key.

evidence.quote: IMPORTANT Posix semaphore names are limited to 31 UTF-8 characters (PSEMNAMLEN) so use a short app group ID and name.
KERN_BOOTTIME will be updated by the system whenever the system clock change.
return timeval2nsec(tv) - boottime;
These assignments require Apple cookies authentication (running locally) as the official App Store Connect API does not support these operations.

verdicts.note: The Shell manifest on main holds WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS. Main sepolicy lets every domain read proc_random and maps /proc/sys/kernel/random to it. The kernel docs define boot_id as fixed for one boot. I also checked the plan's Android 7 floor. In nougat-release, /sys/kernel/random has no label of its own (it falls under generic proc), and untrusted_app.te allows reading proc files, so boot_id is readable on every supported version. No primary source shows 'settings put global boot_count' succeeding on a given build, so medium confidence is right. Since boot_id works on Android 7 and up, BOOT_COUNT is only needed as a fallback if the file read fails.

evidence.quote: allow untrusted_app proc:file r_file_perms;
genfscon proc /sys/kernel/random u:object_r:proc_random:s0
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS" />

verdicts.note: I redid the arithmetic. 2 + 100e-6 x 604,800 = 62.48 s. The allowance reaches 10 s at 80,000 s (22.2 h) and 30 s at 280,000 s (3.24 days). 23 ppm over 7 days is 13.9 s. The Raltron R38 table matches the quote. The TrustedTime quote is paraphrased; the blog's exact wording is below. Most of the impact falls on phones that are offline when scanning, because an online phone refreshes its certificate when the app opens.

evidence.quote: It's important to note that the device's internal clock can drift due to factors like temperature, doze mode, and battery level.
TURNOVER TEMPERATURE 25°C ±5°C

verdicts.note: The RFC 7384 quotes are word for word (Oct 2014). Roughtime draft-19 (17 Mar 2026, Experimental, IESG state 'RFC Ed Queue') contains the nonce sentence and requires the request-to-response delay to stay under a maximum that each implementation chooses. The Apple support page (26 Mar 2025) is quoted word for word. Android's default network security config trusts only system CAs for apps targeting API 24 and up. The severity should be high, not medium. A replayed certificate lets an iPhone student set the computed scan time right next to a forwarded QR's time slot, so the Phase 2 check (line 243) reads 'normal'. A reboot after the scan then removes any second anchor that could contradict it. The fixed 2 s cap is a tuning choice; see recommendation_issues.

evidence.quote: the delay between request and response is within an implementation-dependent maximum value
In a replay attack, an attacker records protocol packets and replays them at a later time without any modification.
Saati doğrulanmış kayıtta QR ile okutma arasındaki fark 10 saniyeye kadar normal sayılır

verdicts.note: Roughtime draft-19 is Experimental and in the RFC Editor queue. It needs at least three servers and runs the query sequence twice. RFC 3161 needs a TSA (Aug 2001). HMAC with Node's built-in crypto is the compact choice and matches the MAC the plan already uses for QR codes (line 247). The Roughtime quote is paraphrased; the exact text is below. The Elson and Römer piggyback quote is exact. One part is wrong: piggybacking does not replace the network-change refresh. A network change triggers no server call unless records are waiting to be sent. The version check runs at most once a day (line 510). Batch uploads of up to 200 records are the responses most likely to exceed F5's 2 s cap.
verdicts.correction: Keep one tiny certificate request (nonce in, HMAC certificate out) when the app opens and when the network changes. Attaching certificates to small responses is a bonus. Do not rely on batch-upload responses to keep anchors fresh.

evidence.quote: The client randomly selects at least three servers from the list, and sequentially queries them.
Uygulama açılışta, günde en çok bir kez kendi sunucuma sorar.

verdicts.note: On iOS, expo-device getUptimeAsync returns ProcessInfo.systemUptime x 1000, and Apple defines systemUptime as awake time. The SDK 57 docs only mention Android. The wording fix is correct.

evidence.quote: return ProcessInfo.processInfo.systemUptime * 1000
The amount of time the system has been awake since the last time it was restarted.

verdicts.note: Plan lines 194, 211, 293 and 315 read as quoted. Line 315 describes one combined rule, while lines 194 and 293 read as two separate limits. This is an ambiguity inside the plan text, so no outside source is needed.

evidence.quote: Saati doğrulanamayan ve yedek kodla alınan kayıtlardan her öğrenci için her derste dönem başına en çok 2 tanesi otomatik kabul edilir.
Yedek kodu iletmek: her derste dönem başına en çok 2

recommendation_issues.problem: This conflicts with the slice's own threat model (F5). The backward anchor is an elapsed time the phone reports, compared with server receipt, with no signature and no freshness bound. An iPhone student with a user-installed root CA can edit the upload or hold it back. After a deliberate reboot before check-in, that value alone sets the record time, and the record would read as verified. Adopt it only with a fresh nonce-bound certificate fetched at upload time and a device-key signature over (record id, certificate, elapsed time).

Nobody has tested the hard 2 s cap. Replies can take longer than 2 s on a cold HTTPS connection over a weak mobile link, or at the class-start peak when up to 20,000 phones open the app. Those phones keep an aging certificate, and their allowance grows toward 62 s, which undermines F4's QR rule. A better approach: read the counter when the request is sent and when the reply arrives, add the measured round trip to the allowance, use a looser cap, and keep the certificate call tiny. Roughtime leaves the maximum delay to each implementation.

The claim that piggybacking replaces the network-change refresh is wrong. No server call happens unless records are waiting to be sent, and the version check runs at most once a day (line 510). Batch-upload replies are also the ones most likely to break F5's 2 s cap. Keep a tiny dedicated certificate call.

misses.plan_quote: Aşama 2'de QR'ın zaman dilimi de saat kanıtı olur.
misses.finding: A QR time slot only proves a lower bound: the scan happened after that QR appeared. It does not show how long after, and a QR forwarded by message carries the same slot. The forwarded-QR check (10 s and 30 s, lines 243 and 291) needs the scan time, which a record with unverified time does not have. Line 251 says the slot is 'saati doğrulanamayan kayıtlar için de kanıt'. If that is built so the slot removes the 'saat doğrulanamadı' label, any student can bypass the forwarded-QR check by rebooting before scanning, which costs nothing and needs no tools. If the label and the 2-record limit stay, the damage is limited to 2 per course per term. The plan does not say which reading applies. Standard time-stamping has the same asymmetry: a server time stamp proves 'existed before', while an unpredictable value proves 'made after'.

evidence.quote: this proves that the signed response could only have been generated after the nonce.
The TSA's role is to time-stamp a datum to establish evidence indicating that a datum existed before a particular time.
Saat kanıtı: QR'ın zaman dilimi, saati doğrulanamayan kayıtlar için de kanıt olur.

misses.recommendation_tr: Satır 194 ve 251'deki cümleyi daraltırım: QR yalnız okutmanın QR ekranda göründükten sonra yapıldığını kanıtlar, ne kadar sonra yapıldığını kanıtlamaz; mesajla iletilen QR da aynı zaman dilimini taşır. Bu yüzden saati doğrulanamayan QR kaydında 10 ve 30 saniye kuralı uygulanamaz; kayıt "saat doğrulanamadı" etiketini korur ve 2'lik sınıra sayılır. Okutma saati gönderim anındaki çapayla doğrulanırsa normal QR kuralları uygulanır.

misses.plan_quote: Böylece kaydın en erken ne zaman verilebileceği kanıtlanır; en geç zamanı da sunucuya ulaştığı an belirler.
misses.finding: Every certificate time and every receipt time comes from the server's own clock, so the whole scheme rests on it. The plan never says how the server keeps correct time or how a wrong clock gets noticed, and the health checks (line 604) only cover the database, the queue and the schema. If the server runs minutes off, every phone's computed time is off by the same amount, so every window opens and closes that far from the real class time. If the server is later stepped back into sync, certificates issued before and after the step disagree by the size of the step. Roughtime, a protocol built for exactly this job, requires servers to bound their own error. Ubuntu has shipped chrony as its default since 25.10.

evidence.quote: Servers MUST ensure that the true time is within (MIDP-RADI, MIDP+RADI) at the moment of processing.
Since Ubuntu 25.10 chrony is used to synchronize time by default.
Sağlık uçları: /health/live (dış bağımlılık yok) ve /health/ready (veritabanı, iş kuyruğu, şema sürümü).

misses.recommendation_tr: Sunucu makinesinin saati chrony ile eşitlenir (Ubuntu 25.10'dan beri varsayılan; üniversitenin kendi zaman sunucusu varsa o da eklenir) ve eşitleme durumu izlemeye eklenir. Bütün saat belgeleri ve "sunucuya ulaştığı an" bu saate dayandığı için eşitleme bozulursa uyarı çıkar ve sunucu yeni saat belgesi vermez; telefonlar eldeki belgeyle devam eder.

misses.plan_quote: Uygulama her açıldığında ve ağ değiştiğinde, internet varsa, saat belgesini yeniler.
misses.finding: Refreshing 'ağ değiştiğinde' (line 192) and sending 'internet gelince' (line 127) both need a listener for network changes, but the phone stack (line 543) names none. Expo SDK 57 already ships expo-network with addNetworkStateListener, so no third-party package is needed. The same listener can drive both the certificate refresh and the send queue.

evidence.quote: Adds a listener that will fire whenever the network state changes.
Expo SDK 57, expo-sqlite ve drizzle, TanStack Query 5, @expo/app-integrity, kendi küçük yerel modülüm

misses.recommendation_tr: "Ağ değiştiğinde" ve "internet gelince" için Expo SDK'nın kendi paketi expo-network kullanılır (addNetworkStateListener); ayrı bir topluluk paketi eklenmez. Aynı dinleyici hem saat belgesini yeniler hem gönderme kuyruğunu tetikler. Teknoloji listesine bu paket yazılır.

misses.plan_quote: iPhone'un gizlilik bildiriminde açılış süresi kullanımı beyan edilir; açılış zamanı telefondan dışarı gönderilmez, yalnız geçen süreler gider.
misses.finding: The sentence ties the privacy declaration to the plan's own counter. Apple's System boot time category, however, lists only ProcessInfo.systemUptime and mach_absolute_time(). Neither CLOCK_MONOTONIC nor F2's semaphore is on that list, so the plan's own module needs no declared reason. The 'only elapsed times leave the phone' rule is therefore a design choice, not an Apple requirement. The records already carry an absolute computed time (line 794). The 35F9.1 entry is still needed because React Native itself uses those APIs; its template declares SystemBootTime 35F9.1. With Expo, the entry goes in ios.privacyManifests.

evidence.quote: The following APIs for accessing the system boot time require reasons for use.
<string>NSPrivacyAccessedAPICategorySystemBootTime</string>
Apple does not correctly parse all the PrivacyInfo files included by static CocoaPods dependencies (such as Expo SDK packages and other ecosystem libraries).

misses.recommendation_tr: Cümleyi düzeltirim: Apple'ın açılış süresi listesinde yalnız systemUptime ve mach_absolute_time var; kendi modülümün kullandığı CLOCK_MONOTONIC ve yeniden başlatma semaforu listede yok, bu yüzden modülüm için ayrı gerekçe gerekmez. 35F9.1 beyanı React Native'in kendi kullanımı için uygulama ayarında (ios.privacyManifests) durur. "Yalnız geçen süreler gider" Apple şartı değil, tasarım tercihi olarak kalır.

verdict_reason: I re-checked all 8 findings against their cited primary sources plus at least one independent source. Six are CONFIRMED (F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, F8) and two are CORRECTED (F1, F6); none is refuted or unverifiable. F1's idea is sound, but as written it trusts an elapsed time the phone reports, unsigned and with no freshness bound. Adopted that way, it would let an iPhone student with a user-installed root CA create a 'verified' late record, so it may only be adopted in the corrected form (fresh nonce-bound certificate plus a device-key signature). F6's claim that piggybacking replaces the network-change refresh is wrong; the HMAC choice itself holds. F5 should be raised to high, because a replayed certificate defeats the Phase 2 forwarded-QR check on iPhone; it is confirmed, so it does not fail the slice. I spot-checked the checked_ok items that carry versions, dates or limits: BOOT_COUNT API 24, play-services-time 16.0.1 (last updated 2025-01-09), TrustedTime on Android 5+, expo-device docs for SDK 57, Apple reason 35F9.1, the Expo privacy page (updated 2026-07-29) and the Raltron R38 figures. There are no disputes. Four misses: two medium (the QR slot only proves a lower bound; the server clock is the unmonitored root of trust) and two low (no network-state listener is named; the privacy declaration is attributed to an API Apple does not list). No high-severity miss remains, so the slice passes. If every corrected recommendation is accepted, the net change in moving parts is 0: TrustedTime goes (-1), expo-network comes in (+1, which line 127 needs anyway), and the App Group is configuration only.
